title: Jazz as a product of place, not race; blues is separate
summary: Rose says jazz came from New Orleans, not from blacks coming north, and that the blues was not fundamental to it. He says New Orleans was a happy town hostile to the blues, and old labels show blues and jazz as separate forms.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: In the first place, in the first place, your general pursuit of this matter reflects certain glaring prejudices, which it is necessary to deal with because they are not exclusively yours. And that is mostly marked by your discussion based on the black man coming north, you see, which is, as far as a jazz form is concerned, a total irrelevancy. Well, wasn't jazz primarily the music of the black American? Of course not. And not only that, but in the process of the coming north, there were quite as many white musicians, possibly more white musicians, involved in the northern trek than black musicians. They were all jazz musicians. They were all faced with identical problems in performance and recognition. The jazz music was not a primarily black form. The jazz music was a product, as I said in a book, of a place and not a race. The phenomenon occurred in New Orleans and, in my opinion, could not have occurred anywhere else. Did not occur here because there were blacks here. That is not to say that blacks didn't make their contribution to the music. They certainly did. But they didn't make their contribution because they were blacks. They made their contribution because they were part of the scene and the music was being produced here. Now, of course, because of definitive failures, that is, failures in definition that are common in the discussions of jazz, people that deal with it, for the most part, have not yet learned to make the distinctions between the many forms of music that in fact took place. There is, for instance, the blues, which is clearly a black form. The assumption that the blues was fundamental to the development of jazz is false. It certainly didn't hurt having it around, did it? No, it didn't hurt having it around, just as it didn't hurt to have any kind of music around, just as the operatic areas that were performed in the French opera found their way into jazz performance, as did the old French quadrilles, which are far more represented in what we think of as the standard jazz material than the blues. And as a matter of fact, in dealing with the blues form as such, New Orleans was fundamentally hostile to the blues. And we never, for instance, here in New Orleans, produced a long line of first-class blues performers or singers. Certainly not those. It never happened. Largely, the reason why it never happened is because in order to produce a phenomenon like the blues, you need to have certain kinds of social conditions. You need to have certain kinds of oppression. You need to have that kind of feeling of people crying out for liberation from their state of living. New Orleans was always a happy town.
